blocks.content: A {{term:kreisdiagramm|pie chart}} shows how a whole is split into a few categories. Each category is drawn as a circle slice with an area proportional to its share. Together all slices add up to exactly 100 %.
A pie slice whose angle (and therefore area) is proportional to the category share of the total. Slices are typically sorted from largest to smallest, starting at "12 o'clock".
Each slice can be labeled with the category name, absolute value, percentage, or a combination. Very small slices are often labeled outside the circle.
When there are many small categories, it is sensible to group them into "Other", otherwise the chart becomes cluttered. A healthy pie chart typically has no more than 5–7 slices.
Pie charts are appropriate for communicating the share of a few clearly distinguishable categories of a whole — e.g. "How does our scrap split across the five defect types?".
More than 7 slices become visually indigestible and small shares are hard to distinguish. Prefer a Pareto chart — it additionally orders categories by size.
The human eye estimates angles and areas poorly. Differences of a few percentage points are barely visible in pie charts. For precise comparisons, use a bar chart.
3D pie charts distort slice areas — front slices look larger than they are. For honest visualization, prefer 2D.

blocks.term: Shares do not add up to 100 %
blocks.content: When categories allow multiple assignments (e.g. "defects with cause A or B"), pie charts are misleading. They assume that categories are mutually exclusive.
Comparing two pie charts side by side is hard — slices move and change order. For comparisons across time or groups, use stacked bars instead.
